project_tagline: A multi-agent content pipeline built on Google ADK, where specialized agents research, plan, write, illustrate and publish, and a deterministic quality gate decides whether they get to stop.
project_description: An internal R&D prototype (never shipped to production) exploring how far a content operation can be handed to a swarm of specialized agents. A monorepo of three services: an ADK agent runtime, a NestJS scheduler and content API, and a Next.js dashboard for batch review. Two orchestration graphs run distinct pipelines: a weekly social pipeline that produces batches of platform-specific posts, and a long-form SEO pipeline that writes MDX blog posts, generates branded hero images and Mermaid diagrams, and publishes drafts to the CMS. The interesting problem was never generation quality on its own. It was control: how to make a non-deterministic system produce output that reliably satisfies hard constraints.
architecture_overview: Two SequentialAgent roots over a shared pool of single-responsibility agents. 'Carl' runs research (Riley) then planning (Maya) then a bounded LoopAgent pairing a writer (Quill) with a quality gate (MayaQA). 'SamBlogPipeline' runs research then a LoopAgent pairing the SEO writer (Sam) with a schema-constrained validator (SamQA). Agents communicate only through ADK outputKey slots in session state (research_brief, content_plan, drafts, qa_result, blog_output) with conversation history disabled, so each stage receives exactly its declared inputs. Deterministic work lives in tools rather than prompts: topic queueing, research retrieval with citations, image generation, Mermaid rendering, published-post registry lookups for internal linking, and CMS publishing.

key_challenges.focus: Never let the model be the quality gate
key_challenges.challenge: The obvious design is an LLM reviewer agent that reads the drafts and decides whether they pass. In practice this fails in the least useful way: the reviewer is as prone to instruction drift as the writer, so a batch with 19 posts instead of 25, or with placeholder text like 'this post will cover...', gets waved through. The pipeline then reports success while producing unusable output.
key_challenges.solution: MayaQA is declared as an agent for orchestration purposes, but its LLM output is discarded entirely. All QA runs programmatically in an afterAgentCallback: exact draft-count assertion, regex detection of placeholder phrasing, and per-platform length thresholds. Generation stays probabilistic; validation is deterministic code. The agent boundary is kept only so the loop can schedule it.

key_challenges.focus: Bounded retry with a machine-readable exit condition
key_challenges.challenge: A write-then-review loop needs a stopping rule. 'Loop until the reviewer is satisfied' either terminates immediately on a lenient pass or never terminates on a strict one, and free-text verdicts cannot be branched on reliably.
key_challenges.solution: SamQA emits a constrained output schema whose verdict is an enum (ALL_PASSED, NEEDS_MINOR_EDITS, NEEDS_REWRITE) alongside structured failure counts. The LoopAgent branches on that enum and is hard-capped at three iterations, so the pipeline always terminates and always terminates with a known state rather than an opinion.

key_challenges.challenge: By default each agent in a chain inherits the accumulated conversation. That bleed is expensive and actively harmful: the writer starts echoing the researcher's phrasing, the QA agent sees the writer's justifications and is anchored by them, and no stage can be tested on its own because its behaviour depends on everything upstream.
key_challenges.solution: Every agent runs with includeContents set to none and reads only its declared state keys. Each stage becomes a pure function of its inputs, which made per-agent smoke harnesses possible and kept token cost flat as the pipeline grew.

key_challenges.challenge: ADK resolves models through its own registry, which makes it easy to hard-wire a pipeline to one vendor. That is a poor bet when model quality, pricing and rate limits move month to month, and it makes it impossible to route different stages to different models.
key_challenges.solution: Wrote a custom LLM connector implementing the ADK model interface and registered it into LLMRegistry, so non-Gemini model strings resolve like first-class citizens. Routing a stage to a different provider becomes a string change rather than a rewrite.
